notes.b: Three words link what is written in DNA to what an organism looks like and does: gene, protein and trait. Getting each one clear is the first step, because exam answers lose marks when they are mixed up.
points: A gene is a section of DNA that contains the instructions, or code, for making a particular protein (strictly, a polypeptide, which is a chain of amino acids). A gene is not itself a protein: it is the recipe for one.

Genes are carried on chromosomes (the long DNA molecules in the nucleus), and each chromosome holds many genes. This is why a cell can make thousands of different proteins from a small number of chromosomes.
A protein is a chain of amino acids folded into a particular shape. About 20 different amino acids are used to make proteins, and different orders of them give different proteins.

A trait is an inherited characteristic of an organism, such as eye colour, blood group, seed shape in peas, or whether a person can make a particular enzyme. The trait is not the protein: it is the visible or measurable result of what the protein does.
notes.tip: If you are asked to define a gene, say it is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. Don't say a gene is a protein, and don't say it is the trait.

notes.b: A gene's code is turned into a working protein in a fixed chain of events. The order of the code decides the protein's shape, and the shape decides what the protein can do.
points: The sequence of bases in a gene (the order of the chemical letters along the DNA) determines the sequence of amino acids in the protein it codes for. Change the order of the bases and the order of amino acids can change.
The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds, and so the protein's three-dimensional shape. This is why every protein folds into its own shape rather than a random tangle.

The shape determines the protein's function, because other molecules can only fit or bind to the right shape. Examples are the active site of an enzyme (the pocket where the reaction happens) and the binding site of a receptor (the spot that a signal molecule attaches to).

The cell's machinery reads the gene. The code is copied into a messenger molecule, mRNA, which travels from the nucleus to a ribosome (a tiny structure that builds proteins), where the amino acids are joined in the correct order.
Information therefore flows in one direction: DNA (gene) → mRNA → protein → trait. There is more on how the copying and joining work in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
notes.tip: Exams ask why the shape of a protein matters. Link the chain: base sequence, then amino acid sequence, then folded shape, then function, such as an enzyme's active site fitting its substrate.

notes.b: Proteins are the link between a gene and a trait because they do most of the work in cells and build much of their structure. Different versions of a gene can therefore give different versions of a trait, and different cells use different genes.
points: Enzymes (proteins that speed up reactions) control the chemical reactions that make substances such as pigments. If the enzyme is missing or faulty, the substance is not made and the trait changes.
Structural proteins build hair, skin, muscle and connective tissue, for example keratin (hair, nails, skin) and collagen (connective tissue, skin, tendons).
Transport and channel proteins move substances, for example across membranes or around the body. Hormones such as insulin, and receptor proteins, carry signals between cells.

Different versions of a gene, called alleles, have slightly different base sequences. They can give a protein with a different amino acid sequence, a different shape, or no working protein at all, which produces a different version of the trait.

Every body cell contains the same genes, but each cell type uses, or expresses, only some of them. For example, the insulin gene is used to make insulin only in cells of the pancreas, and haemoglobin is made only in developing red blood cells.
notes.tip: To explain how a gene controls a characteristic, say the gene codes for a protein and the protein produces the trait, then give an example. For how a change in a gene changes a trait, say the new base sequence gives a different or non-working protein.

notes.h: Worked examples of gene, protein and trait
notes.b: Four examples show the whole chain in action, each as gene → protein → trait. In each one, a change to the protein changes the trait that you can see.
points: Albinism (one form): the gene for the enzyme tyrosinase → tyrosinase is needed to make the dark pigment melanin → people with two non-working copies make little or no melanin, so they have very pale skin, white or very fair hair and light-sensitive eyes.
In albinism the gene codes for the enzyme, not for the pigment: the pigment (melanin) is not a protein, and it is missing only because the enzyme that makes it does not work.

Cystic fibrosis: the CFTR gene → the CFTR protein, a channel in cell membranes that lets chloride ions out of cells → a faulty channel causes thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and pancreas, leading to lung infections and poor digestion.

Haemoglobin: the haemoglobin genes → haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen → normal oxygen transport. There is more on how the change arises in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
A changed form of one of the haemoglobin genes gives sickle-cell haemoglobin, which makes red blood cells sickle-shaped when oxygen is low. This causes sickle-cell anaemia.
Seed shape in peas (Mendel's trait): the gene for starch-branching enzyme → the enzyme helps convert sugar into starch in the developing seed → seeds with a working copy are round.
Seeds with two non-working copies (rr) make less starch and keep more sugar. They take up more water while developing, and so wrinkle as they dry out.
Diagram: DNA (gene) → mRNA → protein (amino acid chain folded into a shape) → trait, with the albinism example written under it.
notes.tip: When asked to explain how a change in a gene changes a trait, pick one example and give all three links: gene, protein, trait. Say it is a non-working enzyme or channel, not a missing pigment gene.

notes.b: The chain from gene to protein to trait is a useful model, but real traits are often more complicated. Genes are not the only thing that shapes an organism.
points: Many traits are controlled by several genes acting together, such as height and skin colour in humans, so there is no single gene for a trait. Each gene adds a small part of the final result.
The environment also affects many traits. A person's height depends on diet as well as genes, and a plant's height depends on light and nutrients.
The trait, or phenotype (what the organism is actually like), results from genes and environment together. This is why two organisms with the same genes can still look different.
notes.tip: Don't write that one gene controls one trait as a rule. If a question mentions height or skin colour, say several genes act together and the environment also has an effect.

keyTerms.definition: A section of DNA that contains the code for making a particular protein.
A chain of amino acids folded into a particular shape, which determines its function.
An inherited characteristic of an organism.
A different version of a gene, with a slightly different base sequence.
The use of a gene to make its protein, so that a cell type shows only some of the traits its genes could produce.
A protein that controls a chemical reaction, such as tyrosinase in the making of melanin.
The observable trait of an organism, which results from its genes and environment together.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between a gene, a protein and a trait.
questions.model: A gene is a section of DNA that contains the code for a particular protein. The base sequence of the gene determines the amino acid sequence of the protein, and the amino acid sequence determines how the chain folds into its shape; the shape determines the protein's function. Proteins such as enzymes, structural proteins and transport proteins do most of the work in cells, so the protein's function produces the trait, for example a pigment made by an enzyme.

questions.prompt: Using one named example, explain how a gene can determine a trait in an organism.
questions.model: Cystic fibrosis: the CFTR gene codes for the CFTR protein, which forms a channel in cell membranes that lets chloride ions out of cells. The base sequence of the gene determines the amino acid sequence of the protein, which determines its shape and so whether the channel works. In people with a faulty gene, the channel does not work properly, causing thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and pancreas, which leads to lung infections and poor digestion. The inherited form of the trait therefore follows from the gene through the protein.

questions.prompt: Identical twins have the same genes but can differ in height. Explain why.
questions.model: Height is controlled by several genes acting together, so there is no single gene for height. The environment also affects height: diet and other conditions during growth can change it. Identical twins share the same genes but may have had different diets and environments, so their height, which is the phenotype produced by genes and environment together, can differ.
